Maimed
MAYMD
adjective
From the Old French mahaignier, “to wound, to mutilate, to cripple,” whence also the noun mayhem; hence deprived of a limb or of the use of one, mutilated, crippled.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To be maimed is to be mutilated — a limb lost or ruined, the body permanently broken. The word runs through the Gospels in three directions, and each is worth having. First, the maimed are healed: “great multitudes came unto him, having with them those that were lame, blind, dumb, maimed, and many others, and cast them down at Jesus' feet; and he healed them” (Mat 15:30), so that the crowd marvelled “when they saw the dumb to speak, the maimed to be whole” (Mat 15:31). Christ restores what sin and a cursed world have torn away. Second, the maimed man is set up as the wise man in the fiercest saying about mortification: “if thy hand offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched” (Mar 9:43; cf. Mat 18:8). The LORD is not commanding self-mutilation; He is measuring hell. If it were literally a choice between a hand and heaven, the hand should go without argument — therefore deal with the beloved sin as ruthlessly as that. Third, the maimed are the guests: “when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind” (Luk 14:13), and when the invited excused themselves the master sent to the streets and lanes for “the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind” (Luk 14:21). The banquet fills with cripples. That is the gospel: the maimed come in, and at the last are made whole.

Webster 1828 Definition

Deprived of a limb or of its use; mutilated, crippled, permanently disabled in the body.

expand to see more

MAIMED, crippled; disabled in a limb; deprived of a necessary part of the body.

From Old French mahaignier, to wound or mutilate — the same root as mayhem.

Christ healed the maimed in multitudes and made them whole (Mat 15:30–31).

Better to enter into life maimed than to go whole into hell (Mar 9:43).

The gospel feast is filled with the poor, the maimed, the halt, and the blind (Luk 14:21).

Key Scripture

Mat 15:30 — "And great multitudes came unto him, having with them those that were lame, blind, dumb, maimed, and many others, and cast them down at Jesus' feet; and he healed them:"

Mat 15:31 — "Insomuch that the multitude wondered, when they saw the dumb to speak, the maimed to be whole, the lame to walk, and the blind to see: and they glorified the God of Israel."

Mar 9:43 — "And if thy hand offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched:"

Luk 14:13 — "But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind:"

Modern Corruption

The mortification texts blunted into metaphor by an age that will not believe in hell, and the feast texts emptied of the repentance that fills them.

expand to see more

Mark 9:43 is among the most softened verses in modern preaching. The reasoning runs that Christ was using hyperbole, and hyperbole may be discounted, and so the saying is reduced to a mild counsel about balance and boundaries. But the figure is hyperbolic only in the surgery; the arithmetic is literal. Christ names the alternative in plain words — hell, and the fire that never shall be quenched — and it is that unquenchable fire which makes the amputation reasonable. Take the everlasting fire away and the verse is madness; leave it in and the verse is common sense. Mortification, then, is not the pruning of excess but the killing of sin: Paul’s mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth (Col 3:5), his if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live (Rom 8:13). Owen said it plainly — be killing sin or it will be killing you.

The feast texts suffer the opposite corruption. Luke 14 is quoted to underwrite a gospel of mere welcome: the master calls the poor, the maimed, the halt, and the blind, therefore Christ receives everyone as they are and requires nothing. But look at the same chapter’s close, where the LORD tells the multitudes that whosoever will not bear his cross and come after Him cannot be His disciple, and bids them count the cost. The maimed are brought in freely, and they are brought in to a table where the Master is Lord. Grace does not consult our qualifications — the guests had none, which is why the invitation had to be free — but grace summons the guest to repentance and to a new obedience. The banquet is not a room where the crippled are congratulated on their crippling; it is the house of the God who at the last will make the maimed whole.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means mutilated or crippled — a body permanently deprived of a limb or its use.

expand to see more

Maimed — Old French mahaignier, “to wound, mutilate, cripple.”

The same root gives English mayhem, the old law-term for maiming a man.

Christ healed the maimed and the multitude glorified the God of Israel (Mat 15:31).

Better maimed in life than whole in hell — the measure of mortification (Mar 9:43).

The gospel feast is stocked with the maimed and the halt (Luk 14:13, 21).

Usage

"The maimed were cast down at Jesus’ feet, and He made them whole."

"Better to enter into life maimed: Christ measures the sin against the fire."

"Call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind — the guest list of grace."
